title: Modeling human performance in running
authors: Morton RH, Fitz-Clarke JR, Banister EW
population: Athletes and non-athletes (running performance); details not given in the abstract
findings: A systematically quantified impulse of training produces dual responses, fitness and fatigue; in the absence of training both decay exponentially with time.
With repetitive training the responses satisfy individual recurrence equations; fitness and fatigue are combined in a simple linear difference equation to predict performance.

A significant observed correlation of model-predicted performance with a measure of actual performance during both training and tapering is presented as validation of the model for athletes and non-athletes alike.
This enables specific model parameters to be estimated and the model to be used to optimise future training regimens for any individual.
limitations: Original formulation; the abstract gives no sample size, parameter values or out-of-sample test. Validation is in-sample correlation. Later work (Hellard 2006, Marchal 2025) shows wide parameter uncertainty and poor identifiability of the fatigue part.
implications: Implement the core engine as a two-compartment exponential impulse-response (fitness minus fatigue) over daily load with per-athlete parameters; do not hard-code population constants as individual truths.

Use it as a descriptive and scenario tool (taper and load-shape what-ifs) and label outputs as model-based estimates; out-of-sample accuracy evidence is weak (see busso-2023-impulse-response-validity, marchal-2025-ffm-statistical-flaws).

verification.notes: Crossref (title, J Appl Physiol, 1990, Morton/Fitz-Clarke/Banister) matches. Europe PMC abstract supports all four findings; no numeric results exist in the abstract.
